title: Linear regression with one feature

sections.title: 4.3 Two ways to find the best line

html:
Purpose. A straight line through data is the simplest model that learns. Logistic regression, neural networks and even LLMs are variations on it, so understand this one fully.

Key ideas

  • The model is f(x) = w x + b. The weight w is the slope and the bias b is the value at x = 0.
  • "Best line" has to be defined. The usual definition: the line that makes the squared gaps to the points as small as possible.
  • You can find that line in one step with a formula (least squares), or step by step with gradient descent (Chapter 6).
  • With one input feature the model is called univariate linear regression.

4.1 The model

Ng's running example predicts a house price from its size, using 47 houses from Portland. Plot size on the horizontal axis and price on the vertical axis, and the points rise to the right. Draw a line through them and you can read off a price for any size: his client's 1,250 square foot house comes out at about $250,000.

fw,b(x)=w x+bf_{w,b}(x) = w\,x + b
  • x is the input (size), and f(x), written y-hat, is the prediction (price).
  • w (weight, slope, coefficient): how much the prediction rises when x rises by 1.
  • b (bias, intercept): the prediction when x is 0.

With w = 0.2 thousand dollars per square foot and b = 0, a 1,250 square foot house gives 1,250 x 0.2 = 250, which is $250,000. Different values of w and b give different lines, and training is the search for the best pair.

4.2 What "best" means

A line can pass close to some points and far from others. To compare lines you need one number that says how far a line is from all the points together. The recipe (Infinite Codes asks you to put each formula into words like this):

  1. For one point, the error is the prediction minus the true value: f(x) - y.
  2. Square it, so that errors above and below the line both count as positive, and big misses count much more than small ones.
  3. Add up the squares over all points.

Take three points (1, 1), (2, 2) and (3, 3). The line with w = 1 and b = 0 passes through all three: every error is 0. The line with w = 0.5 and b = 0 predicts 0.5, 1 and 1.5, so the errors are -0.5, -1 and -1.5. Squared and added, that is 0.25 + 1 + 2.25 = 3.5. The first line is clearly better, and the number says so. Chapter 5 turns this recipe into the cost function.

4.3 Two ways to find the best line

  • A formula (least squares, the normal equation). For linear regression only, calculus gives w and b directly, with no repeated steps. Libraries such as NumPy and scikit-learn use it.
  • Gradient descent. Start anywhere and improve step by step. It is slower here, but it also works for logistic regression and neural networks, where no formula exists.

Code: the formula. Fifty noisy points around the line y = 3x + 2:

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = rng.uniform(0, 10, 50)
y = 3 * x + 2 + rng.normal(0, 1, 50)

A = np.c_[x, np.ones_like(x)]            # a column of x and a column of ones (for b)
w, b = np.linalg.lstsq(A, y, rcond=None)[0]
print(round(w, 3), round(b, 3))            # 3.052 1.757
print(round(w * 4 + b, 2))                 # prediction for x = 4: 13.97

The true values are 3 and 2. The fit finds 3.052 and 1.757, because the noise nudges it. The same data is reused in Chapter 6.

4.4 Using a fitted line well

Beyond the videos.

  • Interpolation is safe, extrapolation is not. The line is only trustworthy inside the range of sizes it saw. A line fitted to houses between 300 and 2,000 square feet says little about a 10,000 square foot mansion.
  • Correlation is not causation. A good fit tells you that size and price move together, not that making a house bigger would raise its value by the slope.
  • Mind the units. If x is in square feet and y in thousands of dollars, w is in thousands of dollars per square foot. A weight is meaningless without its units.

Loan example. Predict the monthly cost of an offer from the offered amount. A fitted model might look like f(amount) = 0.029 x amount + 8 (invented numbers). Then a 10,000 euro offer is predicted at 0.029 x 10,000 + 8 = 298 euros per month. Once you add the number of terms as a second input (Chapter 7), the predictions get much better.

Common mistakes

  • Reading w as "the effect of x" without checking the units or the range.
  • Predicting far outside the range of the training inputs.
  • Forgetting that b exists: a model f(x) = w x forces the line through the origin.

Check yourself

  • For f(x) = 0.2 x + 30, what is the prediction at x = 100, and what does 30 mean?
  • Why do we square the errors instead of just adding them?
  • Why can we not trust a fitted line far outside the data it saw?
Show answers

(1) 0.2 x 100 + 30 = 50; 30 is the prediction at x = 0, the bias. (2) Plain errors above and below the line cancel each other, and squaring also punishes big misses. (3) The relationship may change outside that range, and the data has no evidence about it.
